1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
5	This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).
6	
7	Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
8	Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
9	Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow 1.0$: overall 3-class F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.723; the most affected single generator, Qwen3-1.7B, drops to per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
10	These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).
11	
12	DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.

1	We complement the permutation importance analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) with a leave-one-feature-out ablation. Each row drops one of the seven features and re-evaluates the full 6-gen LOGO protocol; $\Delta$ is the change relative to the full 7-feature ensemble (F1\,=\,0.789).
2	
3	\begin{table}[h]
4	\centering
5	\small
6	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
7	\toprule
8	\textbf{Dropped feature} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ \textbf{vs Full} \\
9	\midrule
10	entropy\_max    & 0.774 & $-$1.50\,pp \\
11	entropy\_mean   & 0.783 & $-$0.63\,pp \\
12	ttr             & 0.784 & $-$0.55\,pp \\
13	hapax\_ratio    & 0.785 & $-$0.42\,pp \\
14	tail\_decay     & 0.786 & $-$0.33\,pp \\
15	entropy\_std    & 0.786 & $-$0.29\,pp \\
16	entropy\_min    & 0.789 & $+$0.01\,pp \\
17	\midrule
18	Full (7 features) & 0.789 & --- \\
19	\bottomrule
20	\end{tabular}
21	\caption{Leave-one-feature-out ablation (6-gen LOGO). Each row drops one feature and re-evaluates with the LOGO protocol. Sorted by impact magnitude.}
22	\label{tab:lofo}
23	\end{table}
24	
25	\paragraph{Analysis.}
26	Entropy\_max causes the largest degradation when removed ($-$1.5\,pp), despite ranking only fourth in permutation importance (split frequency 0.063). This indicates that entropy\_max provides unique signal (capturing the most surprising token under the reference model) that is not redundant with other features.
27	Conversely, entropy\_min is fully redundant ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.01\,pp), consistent with its near-zero permutation importance (0.015).
28	Six of seven features contribute positively to the ensemble, which confirms that the 7-feature design is not over-specified.

This appendix validates the causal predictive power of DDR features through three complementary analyses: permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention.

\paragraph{Permutation Importance.}
Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance} reports the mean F1 drop when each feature's values are randomly shuffled across the test set (baseline F1\,=\,0.771).
Drifting features dominate: their average F1 drop (0.187) is $5.3\times$ larger than the near-stationary average (0.034), confirming that location-shift features---not shape features---drive depth classification.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcr}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Group} & \textbf{Mean F1 Drop} & \textbf{Rank} \\
\midrule
hapax\_ratio  & Drifting      & 0.235 & 1 \\
entropy\_mean & Drifting      & 0.170 & 2 \\
ttr           & Drifting      & 0.156 & 3 \\
entropy\_max  & Near-stat.    & 0.070 & 4 \\
entropy\_std  & Intermediate  & 0.057 & 5 \\
entropy\_min  & Near-stat.    & 0.019 & 6 \\
tail\_decay   & Near-stat.    & 0.014 & 7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Permutation importance (6-gen LOGO). Each feature is shuffled independently; the resulting F1 drop quantifies marginal importance. Drifting features average $0.187$ vs.\ near-stationary $0.034$ ($5.3\times$).}
\label{tab:perm-importance}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger Causality.}
Table~\ref{tab:granger} reports Fisher-combined $p$-values from panel Granger causality tests (lag\,=\,1) across 8 generators ($N$\,=\,29{,}095).
Six of seven features exhibit significant Granger causality ($p < 0.001$), meaning past feature values predict future depth beyond what past depth alone explains.
The sole exception is entropy\_min ($p$\,=\,0.375), providing additional evidence for its near-stationary classification: it carries neither large marginal importance (Table~\ref{tab:perm-importance}, rank 7) nor temporal predictive direction.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Combined $p$} & $\boldsymbol{\Delta R^2}$ & \textbf{Significant} \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & $< 0.001$ & 0.031 & Yes \\
hapax\_ratio  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
ttr           & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_mean & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_max  & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
tail\_decay   & $< 0.001$ & ---   & Yes \\
entropy\_min  & $0.375$   & ---   & No  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Granger causality (Fisher combined across 8 generators, lag\,=\,1, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). $\Delta R^2$ is reported where available.}
\label{tab:granger}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Key Findings.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Drifting dominance.} The $5.3\times$ permutation-importance gap confirms that drifting features (entropy\_mean, ttr, hapax\_ratio) are the primary depth signal carriers, consistent with the DDR partition derived from convergence analysis (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).

\item \textbf{Entropy\_min lacks causal direction.} Beyond its small effect size (F1 drop\,=\,0.019), entropy\_min is the only feature without significant Granger causality ($p$\,=\,0.375). This strengthens the near-stationary classification: the feature is neither marginally important nor temporally predictive.

\item \textbf{Entropy\_max asymmetry.} Entropy\_max ranks fourth in permutation importance (F1 drop\,=\,0.070) but produces the largest degradation in the leave-one-out intervention ($-$2.0\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:lofo}), indicating that it provides unique signal not redundant with other features---its causal contribution exceeds its marginal importance.

\item \textbf{Mistral heterogeneity.} In per-generator Granger tests, Mistral-7B shows non-significant hapax\_ratio and ttr ($p > 0.4$), though Fisher combination across generators remains significant. This generator-specific attenuation partly explains Mistral's lowest LOGO F1 (0.633) and suggests that DDR fingerprints are weaker in models with heavier repetition penalties.
\end{enumerate}
